scope: Six existing PrepVisor technical guides. Current wording is captured from the pre-Phase-5 source where noted; entries record material claims prioritized for review, not every technical sentence.

claims.claim: Availability and latency requirements
claims.currentWording: Redirection lookup must complete in under 20 milliseconds; High Availability (99.99%): Redirection must never drop.
claims.evidenceRequired: Scenario requirements or measured service SLOs; distinguish targets from observed results.
claims.implementation: Relabeled as example targets and removed the implied delivery guarantee.

claims.claim: Capacity estimates and cache fit
claims.currentWording: 100 million writes/month, 100:1 reads, 2x peak, 600 bytes/record, 80/20 cache estimate, and 41.4 GB can comfortably fit in one 64 GB Redis cluster node.
claims.evidenceRequired: Explicitly stated scenario assumptions plus deployment-specific overhead and measurements.
claims.implementation: Labeled traffic and cache figures as assumptions; added excluded overhead caveats and example labels.

claims.claim: HTTP 301/302 caching and analytics behavior
claims.currentWording: 301 is cached locally and prevents analytics; 302 forces all clicks through the server.
claims.evidenceRequired: HTTP semantics standard and caveats for cache directives and client behavior.
claims.implementation: Corrected the FAQ and cited RFC 9110; avoids asserting that either status alone determines analytics.

claims.claim: KGS guarantees zero collisions and instantaneous O(1) writes
claims.currentWording: KGS guarantees zero collision and O(1) instantaneous writes.
claims.evidenceRequired: Uniqueness and allocation invariants in a specified implementation.
claims.implementation: Describes the KGS pattern as conditional on key creation, reservation, and allocation.

claims.claim: Popularity claim naming Google, Meta, and Amazon
claims.currentWording: One of the most classic system design interview problems asked at Google, Meta, and Amazon.
claims.evidenceRequired: Reliable, current, company-specific interview-frequency evidence.
claims.implementation: Removed the frequency and company attribution from the guide summary.

claims.claim: Java concurrency is the #1 filter and ConcurrentHashMap is the single most asked question
claims.currentWording: Java concurrency is the #1 filter; ConcurrentHashMap is the single most frequently asked collections question.
claims.evidenceRequired: Representative interview data; no suitable evidence exists in the repository.
claims.implementation: Removed #1/popularity framing and described the topic as a useful interview-preparation subject.

claims.claim: Virtual thread memory/count capacity and interview frequency
claims.currentWording: In 2026 every senior interview will ask this; virtual threads use a few hundred bytes and one million run comfortably on a standard laptop.
claims.evidenceRequired: Version-specific JDK documentation and workload-specific benchmark conditions.
claims.implementation: Removed interview-frequency, memory, and laptop-scale claims; cited JEP 444 and Oracle's JDK 24 migration guide.

claims.claim: Virtual-thread pinning requires replacing synchronized
claims.currentWording: Blocking in synchronized pins virtual threads; replace synchronized with ReentrantLock.
claims.evidenceRequired: JDK-version documentation for pinning behavior and the application's measured profile.
claims.implementation: Explains JDK 21–23 versus JDK 24 monitor behavior and recommends profiling rather than blanket replacement.

claims.claim: ConcurrentHashMap reads are always lock-free
claims.currentWording: Reads are 100% lock-free; it never locks for read operations.
claims.evidenceRequired: The applicable JDK API contract and implementation details for the version discussed.
claims.implementation: Removed the absolute takeaway; guide references the official JDK API.

claims.claim: Redis Lua scripts execute atomically
claims.currentWording: Lua script execution eliminates check-then-act races.
claims.evidenceRequired: Redis official scripting semantics plus the limits of script-level atomicity.
claims.implementation: Added Redis scripting reference and states that scripts block other server activity while running.

claims.claim: Redis TIME eliminates clock skew
claims.currentWording: Always fetch the canonical timestamp from Redis to eliminate skew.
claims.evidenceRequired: Redis TIME semantics and distributed clock caveats.
claims.implementation: Clarified that it returns time from the handling Redis server, not globally synchronized time; linked official command documentation.

claims.claim: Redis fits 100 million keys on a standard 16 GB node; AWS network utilization is below 1%
claims.currentWording: 64 bytes/key, 6.4 GB total, fits comfortably in a standard cloud Redis node; 60 Mbps is under 1% of standard 10 Gbps EC2.
claims.evidenceRequired: Measured memory footprint, exact Redis service/node type, payload and traffic assumptions.
claims.implementation: Removed the 16 GB node-fit and AWS network-utilization assertions. Retained storage, QPS, and network arithmetic only as explicitly labeled scenario assumptions; validate implementation inputs before using them as a real deployment estimate.

claims.claim: Token Bucket is the industry/default standard
claims.currentWording: Token Bucket is the Industry Standard and default recommendation for modern REST APIs.
claims.evidenceRequired: Scope-specific implementation survey or standards-level basis.
claims.implementation: Describes it as one option where controlled bursts are a requirement.

claims.claim: Rate limiter should always fail open / be placed at gateway
claims.currentWording: Fail-open is recommended for most systems; gateway placement is required.
claims.evidenceRequired: Threat model, downstream capacity and endpoint-specific availability/security priorities.
claims.implementation: Explains fail-open/closed trade-offs and allows edge and service-level limits as appropriate.

claims.claim: Transactional proxy self-invocation and rollback behavior
claims.currentWording: Self-calls bypass proxy interception; default rollback only applies to unchecked exceptions and Errors.
claims.evidenceRequired: Spring framework version docs and proxy mode/rollback configuration caveats.
claims.implementation: Added versioned Spring documentation references; states default behavior and configurable rollback rules.

claims.claim: Virtual threads provide WebFlux-level throughput / tens of thousands of concurrent requests
claims.currentWording: Spring Boot 3.2 virtual threads achieve WebFlux-level throughput and scale to tens of thousands of concurrent requests.
claims.evidenceRequired: Exact Spring Boot/JDK configuration, workload, connection pools, and reproducible benchmark.
claims.implementation: Removed the throughput/concurrency guarantee and described resource and version dependencies.

claims.claim: Outbox guarantees at-least-once delivery with zero inconsistencies
claims.currentWording: CDC guarantees at-least-once delivery with zero data inconsistencies.
claims.evidenceRequired: Chosen database, relay/CDC, broker delivery and recovery semantics.
claims.implementation: Describes dual-write mitigation while noting delivery semantics and recovery depend on the relay/broker.

claims.claim: LRU is a frequent question at named companies; Caffeine reaches tens of millions ops/sec
claims.currentWording: Most frequently asked at Meta, Google, Microsoft, Apple; Caffeine ring-buffer approach achieves tens of millions concurrent operations/sec.
claims.evidenceRequired: Company interview data and a reproducible benchmark for an exact Caffeine version/hardware/workload.
claims.implementation: Removed popularity/company claims; removed the benchmark and made cache concurrency strategy implementation-specific.

claims.claim: Notification capacity and latency targets represent actual scale
claims.currentWording: 100 million notifications/day, 10x peaks, 1 KB records, sub-2-second P0, and 99.99% availability.
claims.evidenceRequired: Clearly labeled scenario assumptions or measured service objectives.
claims.implementation: Labels scope/targets as hypothetical examples; remaining calculation callouts are marked example values.

claims.claim: Queues guarantee zero loss or priority isolation guarantees no delay
claims.currentWording: Queues guarantee zero notification loss; isolated workers ensure zero latency contention and never delay OTPs.
claims.evidenceRequired: End-to-end durability, provider, retry, partition, and shared-resource guarantees.
claims.implementation: Explains queues reduce some failure modes but do not guarantee delivery or zero delay.

claims.claim: Twilio/SendGrid have fixed throughput caps
claims.currentWording: Twilio may restrict to 500 SMS/sec; SendGrid may limit to 1,000/sec.
claims.evidenceRequired: Current provider/account-specific plan and contract documentation.
claims.implementation: Removed fixed rates and directs readers to their account/agreement.

claims.claim: Notification questions are a premier challenge and the guide handles billions
claims.currentWording: A premier system design interview challenge; service capable of billions of notifications.
claims.evidenceRequired: Interview frequency evidence and deployment benchmark.
claims.implementation: Removed popularity and scale claims from title/summary copy where identified.

claims.claim: PrepVisor interactive-canvas evaluation and availability
claims.currentWording: The CTA describes an interactive canvas and immediate AI evaluation of capacity math and bottlenecks.
claims.evidenceRequired: Current product UI and behavior for this exact design exercise and evaluation feedback.
claims.implementation: Removed immediate-evaluation wording; CTA now describes practicing on the existing interactive system design canvas.

claims.claim: PrepVisor concurrency unit tests and real-time Big-O/thread-safety AI feedback
claims.currentWording: The CTA promises multithreaded unit tests and real-time AI feedback.
claims.evidenceRequired: Current coding product behavior for concurrency-specific tests and feedback.
claims.implementation: Replaced with a narrower invitation to practice code patterns and reason through complexity and thread safety.

claims.claim: PrepVisor AI system design evaluation of concurrency bottlenecks
claims.currentWording: The CTA promises evaluation by an AI-powered system design mock interviewer.
claims.evidenceRequired: Current product UI and behavior for this exact scenario and evaluation workflow.
claims.implementation: Reworded as an invitation to explore the design and its trade-offs in the system design studio.

claims.claim: PrepVisor provides real-time senior evaluation
claims.currentWording: The CTA promises real-time senior evaluation from an AI evaluator.
claims.evidenceRequired: Product evidence for response timing and the meaning of senior evaluation; the latter could imply a human expert.
claims.implementation: Removed timing and senior-evaluator assertions from the CTA.

claims.claim: PrepVisor supplies real-time Big-O and edge-case AI feedback
claims.currentWording: The CTA promises real-time Big-O and edge-case feedback from an AI coding evaluator.
claims.evidenceRequired: Current coding product behavior for those exact feedback categories and response timing.
claims.implementation: Reworded to describe practice exercises and reasoning through complexity and edge cases.

claims.claim: PrepVisor supports configuration of Kafka queues in an AI-powered interview studio
claims.currentWording: The CTA promises configuring Kafka priority queues and solving idempotency races in the AI-powered studio.
claims.evidenceRequired: Current product interaction for Kafka-specific queue configuration and automated evaluation.
claims.implementation: Reworded as an invitation to explore architecture and design trade-offs in the system design studio.
